title: Search Trees
body:
The family name for every [[Tree]] whose shape encodes an ordering, so that finding a key is
a walk from the root instead of a scan. The vault's treatments live in
[[INFORMATION STRUCTURES]] and this note does not repeat them: [[Binary Search Tree]] owns the
invariant and the operations, [[Balanced Tree]] owns rotations and the AVL / red-black /
B-tree schemes, [[Heap]] owns the one tree in the group that is *not* a search tree.

## Which structure answers which question

| You need | Use | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| exact-key lookup, nothing else | [[Hash Map]] | $O(1)$ average |
| lookup plus order: ranges, successor, sorted traversal | [[Balanced Tree]] | $O(\log n)$ worst |
| the minimum (or maximum) repeatedly | [[Heap]] | $O(\log n)$ per extract |
| lookup where a node costs a disk read | B-tree, see [[Balanced Tree]] | $O(\log_B n)$ reads |

The last row is the one that separates a self-study reading from the course one. Everything
above it counts comparisons; a B-tree counts **block reads**, so it widens each node until it
fills a disk block and the tree gets shallow instead of narrow. That is why [[File Systems]]
and databases use B-trees rather than binary ones, and it is the same locality argument as
[[Cache]], one rung further down the hierarchy.

## The thing worth noticing

A search tree is a decision tree made concrete. Each node is a comparison, each branch an
answer, and the leaf you land on is the answer to the query, which means the $\log n$ is not
an implementation detail: it is the height of a binary tree with $n$ outcomes, and no
comparison-based search can do better. Exactly the argument that bounds sorting at
$n \log n$ in [[Sequential Sorting]], applied to one query instead of a whole permutation.

Which also says what breaks it. The bound is on *comparisons*, so a structure that looks at
the key's bits or hashes it instead is not bound by it, and that is precisely what
[[Hashing]] and radix structures (tries) do.

## Core Facts to Know

- Search tree = a tree whose shape encodes an ordering, so search descends instead of scanning.
- Height is the cost of every operation, so keeping it near $\log n$ is the whole game.
- Unbalanced BSTs degenerate to $O(n)$ on sorted input; see [[Balanced Tree]].
- B-trees are wide because their cost unit is a disk block, not a comparison.
- A search tree is a decision tree, so $\Omega(\log n)$ comparisons is a lower bound.
- [[Hashing]] beats trees on exact lookup and loses on anything involving order.

> [!note] Not a [[Game Trees|game tree]]
> Both are trees searched from the root and the words get swapped constantly. A search tree
> encodes an **ordering**, so the walk down is a decision about where a key must be. A game tree
> encodes **possibility**, nothing is sorted, and the walk down is enumeration. The cost story is
> opposite too: $O(\log n)$ here, $O(b^d)$ there.
